I said in the title that "I'm having...", as if this were a problem in the last 24 hours, but that isn't true. I have spent a long time reading philosophy, ancient and modern. But over time, I've noticed that many of the ongoing problems in big philosophy tend to reduce down to one very big problem: the notion of progress. Basically, what is your idea about what humans are (or ought) to be doing here. It isn't so much that I'm interested in the ethics of this question, but rather our overall human project. What is the human project? What do you think our destiny is here? This problem has been a nagging splinter even within my own political-level thinking.

There seem to be two major ways of thinking about it, and you realize that our categories of conservative v. liberal aren't accidents. I haven't encountered a single thinker in my reading whose answers don't fundamentally fall on one side of the line or the other. I don't want to turn this post into 50,000 words by doing justice to either side. I'll just try to do a cursory summary of them. They really segregate on the ancient/classic versus the modern view of reality.

(1) Reality as a repeating cycle: nothing new under the sun.

(2) The Hegelian view of reality as a constant evolution.

It pretty much works like this: either the universe is something like a seed, all of its information and potential is already here and we are living it out as repeating cycles. Or our predicament is that every moment and every cycle is truly new. How does this relate to what the meaning of human life is? By simply asking the question about what we are doing here. This is where I struggle. On the one hand, so many of the outcomes of liberal progressivism since the Enlightenment (and certainly more recently) seem so wrong. I watch the movement society is making in the Internet age and the age of high technology. I ask whether the reason that I see it as troubling is because the ways we are using technology are wrong (i.e. tech is neutral), or because the technology itself (and the paradigm it is pulling humanity toward) is itself a bad thing.

The struggle comes when I ask myself: what's the alternative? The impulsive response to the liberal paradigm is, of course, the conservative one. But so many reactionary philosophies wind up being just romantic views of the ancients - always looking backward on a blurry Golden Age. So if we've essentially already "peaked", what is there left to do? It's logically possible that we could return to such a state of humanity, but then I ask - for what? Why are we here? To stay in one place? The only possible way that I see to find meaning in such an existence would be if this reality is merely a stage, preparation for a different form of existence beyond death (it's probably no surprise that in such a paradigm, we find belief in God to be so common - it should press on us that meaning in such a paradigm kind of requires it). Then we can build all kinds of metaphysical systems of morality and politics all based on what we should be doing here - leading to other problems because of the fact that most of those revelations really are taken as revelation from a deity in the literal sense.

The other paradigm says "No", and the person with whom this resonates feels deep inside themselves that there is a destiny for mankind that involves progress. We are moving toward something - regardless of whether our current trajectory is right or wrong. That destiny can't be decoupled from technology - that is, humans being propelled forward through history by solving problems. But this sets me about attempting to really dig into the nature of technology itself. The more that I think about technology's abstract way of separating man from nature and natural law - the more everything starts to adhere to the Jewish ideas about humanity. That our destiny is to overcome the "demiurge", to separate ourselves from the constraints of nature, the Enlightenment ideas of perfectability and the Radiant City.

Both of these paradigms agitate me, but it seems impossible to get away - except to take a post-modern approach to truth, i.e. that Truth isn't. Truth is a linguistic game, an artifact of human meta-language. We know that meaning in this post-modern paradigm is, more or less, an impossibility unless we ourselves become like Gods; we believe that meaning and truth are our job as creative beings to dictate. It's absence in the universe is a vacuum that exists because we haven't created it, and more importantly, enforced it.
